definition:
Providence is God's continuing care for the world he made: he keeps it in being, he works in and through everything that happens in it, and he directs it toward the ends he has purposed. God does not wind the world up and walk away. Rain, harvest, the birth of a child, the rise and fall of kings, and the choices of ordinary people all fall within his governing care, and he works through ordinary events, through human decisions, and even through evil intentions, without becoming the author of evil, to bring about his good purposes. Theologians have traditionally named three aspects of providence: preservation (God upholds all things in existence), concurrence (God acts in and with the real actions of his creatures), and government (God directs all things to their appointed end). They also distinguish general providence, God's care over the whole creation, from special providence, his care for particular persons and events, and ordinary providence, which works through the regular course of things, from extraordinary providence, the miracles in which God acts beyond it. The study of creation treats the act by which God made the world, and the study of sovereignty and human choice treats how God's rule relates to human freedom and to salvation; this study follows how Scripture shows God caring for and governing his world.

The Bible has no single word for providence. The English word comes from the Latin providentia, from providere, ‘to see ahead’ or ‘to provide’. The Hebrew story that best matches it is Genesis 22, where Abraham tells Isaac, “God Himself will provide the lamb” (Genesis 22:8), and then names the place with the words YHWH yir'eh, from ra'ah, ‘to see’, which the BSB renders “The LORD Will Provide” (Genesis 22:14): the LORD sees to it. Job speaks of God's pequddah, his watchful ‘care’ or ‘oversight’, which “has preserved my spirit” (Job 10:12). The Greek pronoia, ‘forethought’, which Greek philosophers used for divine providence, appears in the New Testament only of human foresight, as in Tertullus's flattery of the governor Felix (Acts 24:2). The doctrine rests not on a term but on the Bible's constant witness to what God does.
ot:
Genesis presents God's preserving care from the start. After the flood he promises that “seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall never cease” (Genesis 8:22). He goes with the patriarchs and provides for them, most memorably when he provides a ram in Isaac's place on Mount Moriah (Genesis 22:13-14). The story of Joseph is the Old Testament's great narrative of providence. His brothers sell him out of envy, he is falsely accused and imprisoned, and at each step the narrator says that “the LORD was with Joseph” (Genesis 39:2, 21). When he reveals himself to his brothers in Egypt, he says, “it was to save lives that God sent me before you” and “it was not you who sent me here, but God” (Genesis 45:5, 8). At the end he gives the Bible's classic statement of the doctrine: “As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people” (Genesis 50:20). The same Hebrew verb, chashav, ‘to plan’ or ‘to intend’, is used of the brothers and of God. One event has two intentions; the brothers are guilty of theirs, and God's purpose is good. Joseph neither excuses them nor pretends the evil was good.

The historical books show providence working quietly through what looks like chance. Ruth, a Moabite widow, goes out to glean, and “she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz” (Ruth 2:3); the Hebrew says, in effect, ‘her chance chanced upon’ it, and the narrator lets the reader see the hand that the characters do not. At the end the women of Bethlehem bless the LORD, who has not left Naomi without a redeemer (Ruth 4:14), and the book closes with a genealogy leading to David. When the prophet Micaiah foretold the death of King Ahab, an archer at the battle of Ramoth-gilead “drew his bow without taking special aim” and struck Ahab between the joints of his armor (1 Kings 22:34). Hannah's song confesses that “The LORD sends poverty and wealth; He humbles and He exalts” (1 Samuel 2:7). The book of Esther never mentions God by name in its Hebrew text, yet its reversals, a sleepless king, a gallows turned on its builder, turn on timing no character controls, and Mordecai's word to Esther joins providence and responsibility: “who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14). After the exile, “the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” to let the Jews return (Ezra 1:1; 2 Chronicles 36:22).

The prophets insist that God governs the nations, including those that do not know him. Isaiah calls Assyria “the rod of My anger” (Isaiah 10:5), yet Assyria has its own purpose: “this is not his intention” but rather to destroy (Isaiah 10:7). God will punish the king of Assyria for his arrogance (Isaiah 10:12), for “Does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it?” (Isaiah 10:15). God uses the empire and judges it, both at once. Isaiah even calls the Persian king Cyrus God's “anointed” (Isaiah 45:1). God's purpose stands: “I say, ‘My purpose will stand, and all My good pleasure I will accomplish’” (Isaiah 46:10). Daniel's Nebuchadnezzar, humbled and restored, confesses that God “does as He pleases with the army of heaven and the peoples of the earth” (Daniel 4:35). Lamentations, written among Jerusalem's ruins, asks, “Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?” (Lamentations 3:38), and Amos asks, “If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it?” (Amos 3:6). In Jonah, God “appointed” a great fish, a vine, a worm, and a scorching wind (Jonah 1:17; 4:6-8), the same verb (manah) each time, to teach a reluctant prophet about his mercy.

The Psalms and Wisdom books show providence as daily care. God “makes the grass grow for the livestock” (Psalm 104:14), and “All creatures look to You to give them their food in due season”; when he takes away their breath, they die (Psalm 104:27-29). He “provides food for the animals, and for the young ravens when they call” (Psalm 147:9). The psalmist confesses that “all my days were written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be” (Psalm 139:16). Proverbs holds human planning and divine direction together: “A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps” (Proverbs 16:9), and “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). Even the king's heart “is a waterway in the hand of the LORD” (Proverbs 21:1). Job and Ecclesiastes keep this from becoming a formula. Job's losses come through a heavenly scene he never sees, in which Satan acts only within limits God sets (Job 1:12; 2:6), and his friends' confident explanations are rebuked. God answers Job not with reasons but with a tour of the wild world he feeds and governs (Job 38:39-41), and Job confesses that “no plan of Yours can be thwarted” (Job 42:2). Ecclesiastes observes that from where humans stand, “time and chance happen to all” (Ecclesiastes 9:11). Providence is real, and it is not transparent.
nt:
Jesus teaches providence as the ground of trust. The Father “causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous” (Matthew 5:45). He feeds the birds and clothes the grass, so his children need not be anxious (Matthew 6:26-30), and they are to ask him for their daily bread (Matthew 6:11). “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from the will of your Father. And even the very hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matthew 10:29-30). The Greek says only ‘without your Father’; the BSB, like many translations, supplies ‘the will of’ to make the sense plain, and some readers hear in the shorter form the Father's presence as well as his will. Jesus also refuses to turn providence into an easy explanation of suffering. Asked about eighteen people killed when a tower at Siloam fell, he denies that they were worse sinners than others (Luke 13:4-5), and of a man born blind he says neither the man nor his parents sinned, “but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him” (John 9:3).

The cross is the supreme case of the pattern first seen in Joseph. At Pentecost Peter tells the crowd that Jesus “was delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death” (Acts 2:23). The church prays that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel “carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen” (Acts 4:27-28). The New Testament does not soften either side. The act was lawless and the actors guilty, and it was God's plan for the salvation of the world. Acts goes on to show providence at work in the church's mission: in a storm at sea God promises Paul that no one aboard will die, and yet Paul tells the soldiers, “Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved” (Acts 27:22-31). God's promise and human action do not compete; the promise is kept through the action.

The apostles state the doctrine in its widest form. God “gives everyone life and breath and everything else,” he “determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands,” and “in Him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:25-28), a line Paul quotes from a Greek poet to make a point about the true God. God has not left himself without testimony, since he gives “rain from heaven and fruitful seasons” (Acts 14:17). Christ “is before all things, and in Him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17), and the Son is “upholding all things by His powerful word” (Hebrews 1:3); the verb there, pherō, means to carry or bear along, so the Son is described as bearing creation toward its goal. God “works out everything by the counsel of His will” (Ephesians 1:11). Paul's great promise, “God works all things together for the good of those who love Him” (Romans 8:28), comes in a chapter about groaning, suffering, and persecution, and its ‘good’ is defined by the next verse: to be conformed to the image of the Son (Romans 8:29). Some manuscripts make God the explicit subject and others read ‘all things work together’, but in either reading the good is God's doing. Paul could say that his imprisonment “served to advance the gospel” (Philippians 1:12) and that God's power was made perfect in the weakness he had begged to be rid of (2 Corinthians 12:9).

The apostles also draw out the practical shape of the doctrine. James warns merchants who plan the year ahead as though tomorrow were theirs: “You ought to say, ‘If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that’” (James 4:15). Peter tells believers to cast their anxiety on God “because He cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Paul ends his long reflection on God's purposes in history not with an explanation but with worship: “How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways” (Romans 11:33). In Revelation, only the Lamb who was slain is worthy to open the sealed scroll (Revelation 5:5), an image many interpreters read as the crucified Christ holding the course of history in his hands until its end.

keyTexts.why: Joseph tells his brothers that God sent him to Egypt to preserve life. God's purpose runs through the brothers' crime without excusing it.
What the brothers intended for evil, God intended for good. The Bible's classic statement of providence working through human sin.
Ruth ‘happens’ to glean in the field of Boaz. Providence at work in what looks like chance, seen by the reader but not the characters.
Satan acts only within the limits God sets, and Job blesses the LORD who gives and takes away. Providence reaches suffering, and its reasons are hidden from the sufferer.
All creatures look to God for food and breath, and he renews the face of the earth. Providence as God's daily care for all he made.
A man plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps. Human planning and divine direction held together.
Even the cast lot is decided by the LORD. Nothing is outside God's government, including what seems random.
God uses Assyria as the rod of his anger and then judges it for its arrogance. One event carries God's purpose and the empire's guilt.
Adversity and good both come from the mouth of the Most High. Confessed among the ruins of Jerusalem, not in comfort.
Nebuchadnezzar confesses that God does as he pleases among the peoples of the earth. Providence over empires.
Not a sparrow falls apart from the Father, and every hair is numbered. Jesus makes providence the reason not to fear.
The rulers who crucified Jesus did what God's hand and will had decided beforehand. The cross as the supreme case of providence working through evil.
God gives life and breath to all, sets the times and boundaries of nations, and is not far from anyone. Providence over all peoples.
God works all things together for good for those who love him, and the good is conformity to Christ. Providence tied to salvation's goal.
The Son through whom God made the world upholds all things by his powerful word. Preservation is the work of Christ.

history:
The first Christians taught providence in a world that already argued about it. When Paul spoke in Athens he debated with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers (Acts 17:18). The Stoics taught a rational providence (pronoia) that was close to impersonal fate, and the Epicureans held that the gods, if they existed, took no interest in the world. Early Christian writers rejected both: God is personal, he cares, and his rule does not erase human responsibility. Augustine, in The City of God (written between 413 and 426), argued against both astrology and pagan fate that the rise and fall of empires, Rome included, lies within God's providence, and that God's foreknowledge does not destroy the freedom of human wills. Boethius, imprisoned and awaiting execution, wrote The Consolation of Philosophy (around 524), which distinguished providence, God's plan seen in his eternal present, from fate, its working out in the order of time, and it shaped medieval thinking for centuries. Thomas Aquinas, in the Summa Theologiae (begun around 1265), taught that God's providence extends to every creature and that God governs through secondary causes, giving creatures real causal power, so that the same effect is wholly from God as first cause and wholly from the creature as secondary cause.

The Reformers made providence a source of comfort. Ulrich Zwingli published a treatise on providence in 1530, and John Calvin devoted three chapters of the Institutes (Book I, chapters 16 to 18, final edition 1559) to God's governance of all things, rejecting both chance and a providence of bare foreknowledge, and insisting that God uses evil without being its author. The Belgic Confession (1561, article 13) confesses that nothing happens by chance and that God is not the author of sin, and draws comfort from it. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, questions 27 and 28) describes providence as God's almighty and ever-present power upholding and ruling all things, so that nothing comes by chance but by his fatherly hand, and says the doctrine teaches patience in adversity, thankfulness in blessing, and trust for the future. The Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 5) teaches that God upholds, directs, disposes, and governs all creatures and actions, ordinarily through second causes, and that sinfulness proceeds from the creature and not from God.

Christians have long disagreed about how God's governance relates to free human choices. Within the Roman Catholic Church, the Jesuit Luis de Molina proposed in his Concordia (1588) that God governs through middle knowledge, his knowledge of what free creatures would do in any circumstance, while the Dominican Domingo Báñez held that God moves every creature to act by a physical premotion. After a long papal commission (the congregatio de auxiliis, 1597 to 1607), Pope Paul V allowed both views to be taught and forbade each side to call the other heretical. Among Protestants, Jacobus Arminius (died 1609) and later John Wesley affirmed God's providence over all things while holding that God permits rather than ordains sin, and Wesley preached a sermon On Divine Providence commending the particular care of God for every believer. The sovereignty study and the site's page at /theology/doctrine/sovereignty-and-freedom trace this debate further.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries deism, from Lord Herbert of Cherbury to Matthew Tindal's Christianity as Old as the Creation (1730), accepted a Creator but doubted that he acts in the world beyond its natural laws. Gottfried Leibniz's Theodicy (1710) argued that God had created the best of all possible worlds, and the Lisbon earthquake of 1 November 1755, which killed tens of thousands, prompted Voltaire's Poem on the Lisbon Disaster (1756) and his satire Candide (1759), which mocked that optimism. The twentieth century's wars and the Holocaust pressed the question again. Karl Barth treated providence in Church Dogmatics III/3 (1950) as the Creator's fatherly lordship, known through Christ rather than read off history. Open theism, set out in The Openness of God (1994) by Clark Pinnock and others, proposed that God does not know future free choices exhaustively; theologians of the Reformed, Arminian, and Catholic traditions widely criticized it. The site's full survey of views is at /theology/doctrine/providence, and the problem of evil is treated at /theology/doctrine/problem-of-evil.

differ.view: The Reformed and Thomist account: meticulous providence
differ.body: God ordains and governs everything that comes to pass, including the free choices of his creatures, and he does so through real secondary causes, so that human choices are genuinely human and fully responsible. Defenders from Thomas Aquinas and John Calvin to the Westminster Confession and recent writers such as John Frame and Paul Helm point to Ephesians 1:11, Proverbs 16:33, Genesis 50:20, and Acts 4:27-28. God is not one cause competing with others on the same level, as an author is not a character in his story, so his governing all things does not remove creaturely freedom but establishes it. Evil remains wholly the creature's, and God ordains it only for good ends, a mystery they confess rather than resolve. They hold that only this account gives the believer the full comfort that nothing touches them outside the Father's hand.

differ.view: The Arminian and Wesleyan account: governance with permission
differ.body: God governs all things and knows all things, including the future, but he has given human beings a real freedom to choose otherwise, and he permits much that he does not cause, including sin. Defenders from Jacobus Arminius and John Wesley to Thomas Oden and Roger Olson point to the Bible's pictures of God grieving, pleading, and responding (Genesis 6:6; Isaiah 5:4; Matthew 23:37), and to texts that say God desires all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4). They argue that God's sovereignty is shown in his wise and loving governance of free creatures, and that God can bring good out of evil he permits, as he did with Joseph, without having willed the evil. They hold that only this account protects God's goodness and makes sense of his sincere invitations and his judgment of sin.

differ.view: The Molinist account: providence through middle knowledge
differ.body: God knows not only everything that will happen but everything that any free creature would freely do in any possible circumstance. Using this middle knowledge, he chose to create the world in which his purposes would be accomplished through the free choices of his creatures. Defenders from Luis de Molina (Concordia, 1588) to William Lane Craig, Thomas Flint, and Kenneth Keathley point to texts in which God knows what would have happened, such as David at Keilah (1 Samuel 23:10-13) and Jesus on Tyre and Sidon (Matthew 11:21-23). They argue that this explains how God can govern meticulously, as the Reformed hold, while creatures keep the freedom to choose otherwise that Arminians defend.

errors:
The church has rejected accounts of the world's course that deny either God's rule or his goodness. Fatalism, the ancient Stoic idea of an impersonal fate and its modern forms, replaces the personal Father with a blind necessity that neither loves nor listens; Scripture's God numbers hairs and hears prayer. Deism allows that God made the world but denies that he remains present in it, and naturalism denies that there is anyone to govern it at all; both contradict the Bible's picture of a world upheld moment by moment by the word of the Son. Dualism treats evil as an independent power equal to God, as though history were an undecided contest; Job's opening chapters show even Satan acting only within limits God sets. The opposite distortion makes God the author of sin, erasing the difference between God's purpose and the wicked intentions of those he uses. The Reformed, Lutheran, Catholic, and Wesleyan traditions all reject this, as Genesis 50:20 and Isaiah 10 do by holding the human agents guilty for their own intent.

There are also pastoral distortions. One reads providence as a code that can be deciphered, so that every tragedy is a punishment and every success a reward, the error of Job's friends and of those who questioned Jesus about the tower of Siloam (Luke 13:4-5). Another turns providence into passivity, as though trusting God meant doing nothing; Nehemiah prayed and posted a guard (Nehemiah 4:9), and Paul, promised the survival of everyone aboard, still insisted the sailors stay with the ship. A third uses the doctrine to silence grief with slogans. Scripture gives whole books to lament and never asks sufferers to call evil good; it asks them to trust that God is working through what is evil toward what is good.
life:
The Heidelberg Catechism names what this doctrine does for a believer: patience when things go wrong, gratitude when they go well, and confidence about the future, since nothing can separate them from the Father's love. That confidence is not a claim to know why each thing happens. Joseph understood his story only years later, Job never learned of the heavenly scene, and Paul ended his account of God's ways in wonder rather than explanation. Providence frees a person to act without being crushed by the belief that everything depends on them, and to plan with the humble proviso James teaches, ‘If the Lord is willing’.

It also shapes prayer. Jesus teaches his followers to ask for daily bread from the Father who already feeds the birds, so that prayer becomes the speech of children who depend on their Father rather than an attempt to manage an indifferent universe. And providence gives a way to face evil done to us. Genesis 50:20 does not call the evil good; it says God was at work within it for good. Believers can name wrongs honestly, grieve them, and still expect that the God who turned the cross into the world's salvation has not let go of their lives.
questions: In Genesis 50:20 the same verb describes the brothers' intention and God's. How does that verse help you think about evil done to you, without calling the evil good?

Jesus says not a sparrow falls apart from the Father, yet he refuses to explain the Siloam tragedy as punishment. How do both of those teachings shape the way Christians should speak to people who are suffering?

Paul was promised that everyone on the ship would survive, yet he insisted that the sailors stay aboard. What does that story suggest about how trust in providence relates to planning, effort, and prayer?
